title: Dimensionality Reduction — t-SNE & UMAP
summary: Modern nonlinear visualization techniques that go where PCA can't — and why their beautiful-looking plots are easy to misread.

slides.markdown:
PCA only finds **linear** directions of variance — it can't unroll a spiral or separate two intertwined clusters that curve around each other.

**t-SNE** and **UMAP** are nonlinear techniques built for one job: squashing high-dimensional data into 2D or 3D for humans to *look at*. They're visualization tools first, not general-purpose preprocessing steps.

slides.subTitle: Nonlinear structure
slides.markdown:
Imagine data shaped like a Swiss roll — a 2D sheet curled into a 3D spiral. Its true structure is 2D, but that structure only becomes visible if you **unroll** the spiral, which is a nonlinear operation. PCA can only project along straight lines, so it flattens the spiral by squashing it, mixing points that were actually far apart along the sheet.

That's the gap t-SNE and UMAP fill: they preserve the *local* neighborhood structure of the data even when the true shape is curved or twisted.

slides.subTitle: Preserving local neighborhoods
slides.markdown:
**t-SNE** (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) converts high-dimensional distances into probabilities of being neighbors, then arranges points in 2D so that neighbors in the original space stay neighbors in the plot — points that were close stay close; it doesn't try hard to preserve distances between far-apart points.

That local-only focus is exactly why t-SNE plots often show crisp, well-separated blobs even on messy real-world data — it's built to make local structure visible, at the cost of global structure.

slides.subTitle: Over-reading t-SNE plots
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This t-SNE cluster is bigger, so that group has more real-world spread — and clusters that are far apart in the plot are truly dissimilar."

**Why it's wrong:** t-SNE only optimizes for keeping *close* points close. Cluster **size**, **density**, and the **distance between separate clusters** in the final plot carry no reliable meaning — they're artifacts of the optimization, not measurements.

**Correct model:** use a t-SNE plot to answer "are these points grouped with these other points?" — never "how far apart are group A and group B, really?"

slides.subTitle: Faster, more global structure
slides.markdown:
**UMAP** (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) targets the same goal as t-SNE — a low-dimensional layout that preserves neighborhoods — but with a different mathematical foundation that runs meaningfully faster and scales to much larger datasets.

UMAP also tends to preserve more of the **global** layout (roughly how far apart distinct clusters really are), which makes it a somewhat safer visualization and, unlike t-SNE, a more reasonable choice as an actual preprocessing step before a downstream model.

| | PCA | t-SNE | UMAP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Structure captured | Linear | Local (nonlinear) | Local + some global (nonlinear) |
| Speed | Fast | Slow on large data | Faster than t-SNE |
| Deterministic | Yes | No (stochastic) | Mostly, with a fixed seed |
| Safe as preprocessing | Yes | No — visualization only | More reasonable, still caution advised |

**How to decide:** use PCA when speed and interpretability of variance matter; use t-SNE purely to eyeball local groupings; reach for UMAP when you want a nonlinear view that's faster and less misleading about global layout.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: perplexity, the parameter that reshapes the plot
slides.markdown:
t-SNE's **perplexity** parameter roughly sets how many neighbors each point considers when deciding what's "local" — typical values run 5 to 50. A perplexity of 5 on a 10,000-point dataset produces many small, tight, fragmented-looking clusters; a perplexity of 50 on the same data can merge those same groups into fewer, larger blobs.

The same underlying data can produce visibly different-looking cluster counts and shapes purely from this one knob — which is why a single t-SNE plot should never be treated as a definitive picture of the data's structure. Standard practice is running t-SNE at a few different perplexity values and checking which groupings are stable across them, rather than trusting any single run's cluster count.

slides.sectionTitle: Why t-SNE and UMAP plots change between runs
slides.markdown:
Both algorithms start from a random initialization and optimize iteratively, so two runs on identical data with different random seeds can produce plots that are rotated, mirrored, or otherwise rearranged relative to each other — the local groupings tend to stay the same, but their absolute position and orientation in the 2D plane don't.

This is a direct consequence of the local-only objective: nothing in t-SNE's loss function cares about absolute position, only relative neighborhoods, so there's no reason to expect two runs to land in the same orientation. Fixing the random seed makes a single analysis reproducible, but doesn't make the layout meaningful in any absolute sense.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: using t-SNE/UMAP output as model input
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I ran t-SNE down to 2 dimensions, so I can feed those 2 coordinates into a downstream classifier instead of the original features."

**Why it's wrong:** t-SNE has no `transform()` for new points — you can't cleanly project a new data point into an existing t-SNE embedding without rerunning the whole algorithm, and its coordinates preserve local neighbor relationships, not a stable, meaningful metric space a classifier's decision boundary could reason about consistently.

**Correct model:** treat t-SNE strictly as a visualization endpoint for humans. If a genuine nonlinear dimensionality-reduction step is needed before a downstream model, UMAP is the more defensible choice (it does support transforming new points), but even then, validate that it actually improves the downstream task rather than assuming it will.
